name: french chicken soup
instructions:
BUILD THE FLAVOR BASE: two valid builds — LEEK/CELERY/CARROT/GARLIC + ONION POWDER, or ONION/CELERY/CARROT/GARLIC (see notes). Finely chop the alliums plus a fraction of the celery and carrots; the garlic is FRESH, minced into the base. Sautee in a GENEROUS amount of BUTTER (with olive oil to raise the smoke point) until softened. Butter is non-negotiable in the base — see notes on why the earlier olive-oil-first framing was wrong.

SEAR THE CHICKEN: add chicken thighs to the pot and sear well.

DEGLAZE WITH WHITE WINE: pour in a generous splash of white wine and let it reduce briefly. The more wine the better — this is the biggest flavor builder.

ADD BROTH: add stock or msg-rich bouillon cubes dissolved in water. Either works, but msg-rich bouillon is genuinely helpful here — this is a broth, not a sauce.

ADD THE SOUP VEGETABLES: chop the remaining carrots and celery very coarse (much bigger than the base — fork-pickup size). Throw them in the pot along with celery leaves and the bulbs of some scallions. These are soup vegetables now, not flavor base.

HERBS: stir in a generous amount of SAGE (fresh is better; powdered will do) and HERBES DE PROVENCE — the two seasonings for this dish, piled on liberally. SKIP rosemary, thyme, tarragon, and parsley, even though those are often canonical (see notes). You need real herb presence here or the broth reads flat and muddy. Onion powder goes in at this stage IF USING LEEKS (see notes). Garlic is fresh in the base, not powdered.

DUMPLINGS: meanwhile, knead a quick dough of all-purpose flour and MILK (not water — see notes). Cut into small balls and drop into the simmering broth in the last several minutes of cook. See [[drop-dumplings]] for the fully-fleshed-out milk-based dumpling with baking powder.

THICKEN WITH BEURRE MANIE TO TASTE: whisk cold butter and flour together into a paste (see beurre-manie recipe), then whisk small amounts of the beurre manie into the simmering broth toward the end of the cook. Add gradually and taste — the goal isn't a full gravy, it's just enough body and butter-flavor lift to keep the broth from reading flat. Amount is entirely to taste; the dish is dramatically flatter without any beurre manie at all than with even a small addition.

FINISH: optional fresh-herb garnish — fresh chives or thinly-sliced green onion tops scattered on top before serving. See notes: fresh garnish is attractive but the dried herb stack does the flavor work.
notes:
TARGET DISH SHAPE — BROTH AS MEDIUM, FORK-EATABLE BITS AS THE MEAL: this is not a spoon-up soup like an indian dal or italian grandma soup. It's a salty broth with discrete components — chicken bits, coarse carrots and celery, scallion bulbs, dumplings — that you pull out individually with a fork. You are not expected to drink the broth. The broth is the seasoning medium; the chunks are what you eat. The whole ingredient list flows from this idea.

BIGGEST FLAVOR BUILDERS — WHITE WINE AND THE DRIED SEASONINGS: the white wine is the most important builder — more is better. The dried seasonings (SAGE + HERBES DE PROVENCE) carry the dish; without them the broth reads flat and muddy.

BUTTER IS NON-NEGOTIABLE AND BEURRE MANIE IS TO TASTE — WITHOUT THEM THE DISH IS FLAT: this is the biggest recipe reversal. Earlier versions of this recipe framed olive oil as the primary fat and butter/beurre manie as optional secondary moves. That was wrong. Without butter as the base fat AND some amount of beurre manie whisked into the broth, the finished soup reads dramatically flat — the salt-and-herb-forward broth has no dairy backbone to sit on and the whole dish comes across as thin.
- BUTTER IN THE SAUTEE BASE — REQUIRED, NOT OPTIONAL: soften the leeks/onions/celery/carrots in butter (with olive oil cut in to raise smoke point and add volume). Butter's dairy fat integrates into the broth in a way olive oil alone can't — it carries the salt and dried-herb flavors on a rich base rather than letting them float in a lean liquid.
- BEURRE MANIE — AMOUNT ENTIRELY TO TASTE, BUT SOME IS REQUIRED: whisk cold butter and flour together (see beurre-manie recipe), then add small amounts to the simmering broth toward the end and taste as you go. The goal is NOT a full gravy (that's chicken pot pie's role — see below). The goal is just enough body and dairy-flavor lift to make the broth taste of something. A small amount goes a long way; err on the light side and add more if you want more body. But no beurre manie at all is a real downgrade — the difference between 'no beurre manie' and 'even a tiny bit' is much bigger than the difference between 'a tiny bit' and 'a lot.'
- OLIVE OIL STAYS SECONDARY AS A BUTTER-CUTTING FAT: olive oil isn't gone, but its role has demoted — it's used alongside butter to raise the smoke point in the sauté, not as the primary fat. Straight-olive-oil versions of this soup are the flat-broth failure mode.

ADD FLOUR TO THE CHICKEN AND VEGETABLES BEFORE DEGLAZING — FOR FLAVOR AND BODY: dust flour onto the seared chicken and softened base vegetables before pouring in the white wine. The flour adds flavor (toasted-flour depth) and integrates with the butter to build early body in the broth. This works alongside the beurre manie added later — the flour-during-sauté is a first pass and the beurre-manie-at-end is a second pass, both contributing body and buttery depth. With butter (not olive oil) as the base fat, the flour + butter combination reads as a proper light roux — that's the right direction, not something to avoid.

NO HEAVY CREAM (CLASHING): cream is the right move for chicken pot pie filling (gravy), but here we're making a broth to eat things out of, not a sauce to bind things together. Cream muddies the clear broth.

NO PEAS, WHITE BEANS, OR LENTILS (CLASHING): all three are spoon-up foods. Even peas — bite sized but you still scoop them with broth. The high-MSG broth doesn't work with spoon-pickup eating; you'd be drinking the broth alongside the legumes, which is the wrong mouth experience. Peas belong in chicken pot pie (where the gravy is fully consumed inside the pie); white beans and lentils belong in stock-forward soups. They are wrong here.

BOUILLON IS OK HERE — UNUSUAL: most cookbook bean and vegetable soups treat bouillon as an antipattern. This dish is the opposite case: it's a broth-meal, and MSG-rich bouillon gives the salty backbone the dish actually wants. Liquid stock works too but you don't need the gentle layered character — punchy salt and umami are correct.

SEASONINGS — SAGE + HERBES DE PROVENCE ONLY: settled. Stick to DRIED SAGE and HERBES DE PROVENCE; SKIP ROSEMARY, THYME, TARRAGON, AND PARSLEY — even though those are often canonical for a french chicken soup. (The sage want-to-try graduated: the blend's sage component was indeed the load-bearing part, so standalone sage joins the blend as the two-seasoning stack.) Dried over fresh remains right for this broth-meal format — concentrated, not delicate.

HERB HISTORY: earlier versions piled on dill/tarragon/oregano (walked back — the fine-herb stack belongs in [[chicken-salad]] and [[chicken-with-vinegar]]), then rosemary + thyme + herbes de provence (also walked back — see SEASONINGS above). Dill stays CLASHING — its bright grassiness fights the broth. Tarragon and parsley are simply skipped now, alongside rosemary and thyme.

WHY SAGE + HERBES DE PROVENCE: herbes de provence's load-bearing components here were always the sage and lavender — what pushes the broth from generic-savory-chicken into something specifically french and floral-warm. Standalone sage doubles down on exactly that component; the blend fills in the floral rest. FRESH SAGE IS BETTER — powdered will do. (Same pattern as [[porkchops-with-a-sauce]]: powdered sage loses its funk.)

FRESH HERBS AND GREEN ONION TOPS ARE GARNISH — DRIED HERBS BUILD FLAVOR: fresh chives and thinly-sliced green onion tops make an attractive garnish scattered on the finished bowl — they add color and a fresh aromatic pop that dried herbs can't. But they DON'T build flavor into the broth the way dried herbs do. Fresh herbs cooked into the simmer wilt and turn dull; their oils are too delicate for the long broth-cook. The dried stack (rosemary + thyme + herbes de provence) is what makes the broth taste of anything. Treat fresh garnish as visual/aromatic only — a finishing scatter on top after the pour, not an ingredient in the pot.

YELLOW ONIONS CAN REPLACE OR AUGMENT LEEKS — I OFTEN PREFER ONIONS: raw yellow onions in the flavor base — a previously-forbidden move in this recipe — actually work well here. I often prefer the onion character to leeks in this soup; onions add a sharp savory backbone that leeks don't, and the sharpness lifts the broth. You can use yellow onions alongside leeks (both in the finely-chopped sauté base) or replace leeks with yellow onions entirely. Leeks are still fine and traditional; onions are a real and often better option.

ALLIUMS — TWO VALID BASES, FRESH GARLIC IN BOTH: either LEEK/CELERY/CARROT/GARLIC + ONION POWDER, or ONION/CELERY/CARROT/GARLIC. Either is fine. The onion powder belongs only to the leek build (it fills the sharp-allium slot leeks leave open; with yellow onions it's redundant). GARLIC IS FRESH — minced into the sauté base — not garlic powder.

DROP DUMPLINGS + CHICKEN THIGH — NO POTATOES, NO TURNIPS: the dish should stick to [[drop-dumplings]] and chicken thigh as its substance. TURNIPS AND POTATOES WOULD DO POORLY here (clashing) — the earlier potatoes-in-a-pinch allowance is withdrawn. Dumplings take on the broth flavor in a way root vegetables don't, and roots muddy the clear fork-pickup format. Egg noodles and pasta remain wrong too (that's a noodle soup, a different dish). Potatoes and peas belong in [[chicken-pot-pie]] — that side of the family.

WATER + FLOUR DUMPLINGS DON'T WORK — USE MILK: the naive plan of just kneading flour and water into small balls is well-reasoned in theory (simplest possible dumpling) but it doesn't actually work in practice. Even with a heavy hand on baking powder, water + flour dumplings come out too dense — they read as leaden little lumps of raw dough that never lighten. Milk is the way, even though the dough gets stickier and harder to shape by hand. The fat and sugar in the milk are load-bearing for the texture — they give you the tender fluffy chewy dumpling this dish wants. See the biscuit-style dumplings recipe for the full milk + butter + baking powder + salt + sugar version, which is the fully-fleshed-out target.

NO MUDDY GREENS (SPINACH, MIXED GREENS, ARUGULA) — WANT SHARP NOT MUDDY: leafy greens kill the clear sharp broth quality. Scallion bulbs, chives, and the herbs already provide the green notes.

COARSE CHOP THE SOUP VEGETABLES, FINE CHOP THE BASE: the carrots and celery that go in as soup vegetables should be large fork-pickup chunks — they're a meal component. The fraction that goes into the sautee base is finely chopped — that fraction is flavor only. Two roles for the same vegetable; two cuts.

DIFFERENTIATION FROM ROSEMARY CHICKEN POT PIE: same starter vegetables (leeks, celery, carrots), same chicken, same white wine. BOTH now use butter and beurre manie — the earlier framing that beurre manie was pot-pie-only was wrong (see butter/beurre-manie note above). But pot pie wants cream + peas + potatoes + FULL beurre manie gravy + crust — a contained thick gravy filling consumed inside pastry. French chicken soup wants broth + bouillon + dumplings + scallions + tarragon + LIGHT beurre manie — a salty butter-and-herb-forward broth with discrete eat-with-a-fork pieces submerged. The beurre manie amount is the axis: heavy = pot pie, light = this soup. Different formats, different amounts, same technique.
